newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian fine wool price surges, IWS says.
newsitem.headline: Australian fine wool price surges, IWS says.

text.p: A sharp increase in demand for fine wool from Europe and Asia combined with concerns about supply produced a 29 percent rise in the price of 19 micron wool since December, the International Wool Secretariat (IWS) said.
However, prices of broader wools of 23 micron and above had risen more slowly, IWS said in its monthly market briefing.
With the exception of fine wool, only a modest pick up in textile fibre prices was expected in the medium-term, it said.
Most fine wool markets entered a re-stocking phase from mid-1996 and Australian exports of 19.5 micron and finer wool for July to March in the 1996/97 season jumped by 30 percent.
This compared with a 17.0 percent rise for total wool exports, the IWS said.
Italy remained the leading export destination for Australian 19.5 micron and finer wool, with China the second largest.
Australia's fine wool exports to South Korea rose by 69 percent in the period, while total wool exports to Korea declined by five percent, it said.

Structural change in Japan's wool industry had brought a shift from direct imports from Australia to wool top imports from Southeast Asia and intermediate and end-product imports from China and Italy, it said.
In the season to May 30 this year, the average price of 19 micron fine wool increased by seven percent year-on-year, the IWS said.
In contrast, average prices for 22 micron and broader wool declined.
Despite a forecast fall in total wool production in Australia this season from 1995/96, auction sales of fine wool of 19.5 micron and finer to May 2 rose by 41.0 percent.
In particular, the sale of 16.5 micron and finer wool increased by 255 percent in the period, it said.
In response to rising auction prices, growers had released stocks of fine wool that had been held over from last season when prices were lower, it said.
Total Australian wool production for the 1997/98 season was forecast to rise marginally to 645 million kg from 639 million kg, it said.
However, the supply of fine wool onto the market next season should remain at current levels or fall slightly, it said.
The availability of fine wool held in broker stores and on-farm was expected to be lower because of the recent run-down in these stocks, it said.
World fibre demand was improving slowly but textile fibre producers were expecting only a modest rise in prices because over-supply was depressing potential price rises, it said.
Excess supply was keeping polyester staple prices under pressure, with prices falling further in April, it said.
Demand for acrylic remained firm and modest price increases in the medium-term were likely, it said.
Forecasts for cotton prices in the 1997/98 season range from a small decline to a two percent rise.
Cotton production was expected to fall compared weith 1996/97 but weak demand should keep prices in check, IWS said.
Global demand for viscose fibres was reported to have fallen eight percent last year to bring prices to their lowest level since 1990.
No improvement was expected this year because of rapid capacity expansion in Asia, it said.
